paragraphs.heading: South Lambeth street, not Marylebone
paragraphs.text: The workbook explicitly places William Loyd (1770–1828) at “13 Portland Place, Clapham Road.” This should not be confused with the better-known Portland Place in Marylebone. A 1919 London County directory locates Portland Place North in South Lambeth, running from 198 Clapham Road to Lansdowne Road. A London Picture Archive description says the Portland Grove estate, formerly Portland Place North, was divided into building-lease plots between 1822 and 1830, with house-building requirements and new roads. This establishes a plausible contemporary street development during the final years of William’s life, not his residence at No. 13.

paragraphs.heading: The number exists later; the family link is unverified
paragraphs.text: Stockwell War Memorial’s local research reports the 1911 census placing Geoffrey William John Dee’s family at 13 Portland Place North. That verifies later use of the numbered address in this street, but concerns another family roughly eight decades after William’s death. The reviewed sources do not show that No. 13 existed in his lifetime or connect him to the later address.

timeline.text: The Portland Grove/Portland Place North estate was laid out through building leases requiring houses and new roads, according to the London Picture Archive description. This does not establish William Loyd’s occupancy.

name: 2 Carlton Gardens
summary: The workbook records Lord Overstone and subsequently Lord and Lady Wantage at 2 Carlton Gardens, their London residence.
connection: The workbook records Lord Overstone and subsequently Lord and Lady Wantage at 2 Carlton Gardens, their London residence.
status: Survives as a Grade II* listed townhouse and is the published address of the Institute for Government.

paragraphs.heading: The family connection
paragraphs.text: The workbook records Lord Overstone and subsequently Lord and Lady Wantage at 2 Carlton Gardens, their London residence.

paragraphs.heading: The London family house
paragraphs.text: The 1905 catalogue of Lord and Lady Wantage’s pictures explicitly includes 2 Carlton Gardens among the collection’s locations, alongside Lockinge, Overstone and Ardington. It provides contemporary evidence for the house’s place in the family’s cultural life.

paragraphs.heading: Architecture and later use
paragraphs.text: Historic England dates the house to about 1828 and attributes it to John Nash with James Pennethorne. It is one of a pair of grand stucco townhouses facing towards the Mall, with an Ionic entrance porch. The Institute for Government currently gives the building as its address. Occupation by the institute does not establish freehold ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Kitchener’s wartime residence
paragraphs.text: The London Archives dates Lord Kitchener’s occupation as Secretary of State for War to August 1914–February 1915. This is more specific than Historic England’s broader 1914–1916 statement, so the exact duration is treated as a source discrepancy rather than extending his residence to his death.

paragraphs.heading: Post-war adaptation
paragraphs.text: A Commons answer on 13 December 1960 records plans to restore and alter the interior for use principally by the Royal Fine Art Commission. The minister hoped to award the contract in summer 1961 and finish in autumn 1962. This is direct evidence of the proposed public use and programme; it does not establish that completion occurred on schedule.

paragraphs.heading: Photographic record of the façade
paragraphs.text: The London Archives catalogue has a property-specific photograph record for the front of 2 Carlton Gardens, confirming the subject building and its archival documentation. The image record’s stated reproduction terms require an Archive licence; the photograph itself is not treated here as reusable.

name: 43 Lothbury
summary: Lewis Loyd lived at 43 Lothbury; the workbook records his son Samuel Jones Loyd’s birth there in 1796.
connection: Lewis Loyd lived at 43 Lothbury; the workbook records his son Samuel Jones Loyd’s birth there in 1796.
status: The historic banking address is verified. NatWest’s institutional history places the site of No. 43 within the larger bank redevelopment completed in 1932; no surviving fabric of the original family home has been verified.

paragraphs.heading: The family connection
paragraphs.text: Lewis Loyd lived at 43 Lothbury; the workbook records his son Samuel Jones Loyd’s birth there in 1796.

paragraphs.heading: Family home and banking address
paragraphs.text: The Illustrated London Almanack for 1851 lists Jones, Loyd & Co. at 43 Lothbury. A history of the neighbouring London and Westminster Bank, preserved in the Business Archives Council material at Glasgow University, likewise identifies Jones Loyd’s premises at number 43 and discusses the bank’s absorption. This supports a business connection as well as the residence recorded by the family. It does not mean the present building at that address is the eighteenth-century home.

paragraphs.heading: The bank’s eighteenth-century beginnings
paragraphs.text: NatWest’s institutional history dates the bank’s foundation to about 1784 as a London offshoot of the Manchester firm. After Watling Street and Walbrook, it moved to Lothbury around 1788. The Loyd name appears in the partnership’s recorded titles from 1793; Jones, Loyd & Co became the name in 1808. The Manchester connection ended in 1848 and London & Westminster Bank acquired the business in 1864.

paragraphs.heading: Surviving records of the premises
paragraphs.text: NatWest catalogues undated Lothbury architectural plans under archive code JON, alongside partnership agreements, correspondence and the 1864 amalgamation papers. These are specific surviving research materials, but their catalogue descriptions are not a substitute for inspecting the plans. Their contents have not been used to infer the layout or survival of the original family home.

paragraphs.heading: A satirical view of the banker
paragraphs.text: The National Portrait Gallery’s archive record for “A view in Lothbury” describes a hand-coloured etching dated about 1817–25 and identifies Samuel Jones Loyd in its title. It supplies a period view linked to his street and business context, but does not identify No. 43 as the building depicted.

paragraphs.heading: Two rebuildings, not one unchanged family house
paragraphs.text: Architectural historian John Booker identifies a rebuilding of the bank’s front by George Maddox around 1808, retaining banking space below and domestic accommodation above. He dates P. C. Hardwick’s later replacement to 1857. These successive designs explain why a Victorian image of Jones, Loyd & Co cannot simply be labelled as the house in which Samuel was born in 1796.

paragraphs.heading: The early house survives in drawings
paragraphs.text: Booker’s illustrated volume reproduces both the earlier townhouse and the later street elevation, with No. 43 labelled beside the London & Westminster Bank. The earlier drawing’s caption says Samuel was born either here or in adjoining No. 44, where a first-floor bedroom appears on a plan. That qualification is retained alongside the workbook’s more definite No. 43. The images can be examined in the linked thesis; they are not modern photographs.

paragraphs.heading: Later tenants, war damage and the enlarged bank
paragraphs.text: NatWest’s 1984 anniversary history says No. 43 was initially let after the takeover. It records the Swiss Bank in Jones Loyd’s former premises when a bombing raid in July 1917 damaged the neighbouring banking hall’s glass roof. Later, the vacant No. 43 formed part of the larger site assembled for the Mewes and Davis rebuilding, completed in February 1932. This institutional account traces the subsequent site history; it does not identify surviving fabric from the Loyd family home.

name: 7 Bread Street
summary: The workbook records William Loyd (1770–1828, family number 4), a warehouseman, at 7 Bread Street before his move to Clapham Road.
connection: The workbook records William Loyd (1770–1828, family number 4), a warehouseman, at 7 Bread Street before his move to Clapham Road.
status: The historical address is preserved in the family record; its exact surviving building or replacement has not been verified.

paragraphs.heading: A City address without a building match
paragraphs.text: The workbook records William Loyd (1770–1828), a warehouseman, at 7 Bread Street. An 1818 commercial guide describes Bread Street, Cheapside as a 68-house street and lists many wholesale and warehouse businesses, establishing the commercial character of the street. Its surviving online transcription does not identify Loyd or establish that its numbered premises correspond to the workbook’s address. A 1720 ward-map catalogue record covers the broad area but is not detailed enough to locate a particular house.

paragraphs.heading: What remains unresolved
paragraphs.text: The searches did not establish whether “7 Bread Street” was a dwelling, business premises, or both, nor whether the number can be matched to a surviving footprint after later street changes. The family record supports an address association; it does not prove ownership. No later occupier or modern building has been assigned to William.

paragraphs.heading: Why the family papers leave a gap
paragraphs.text: The workbook reports that William’s son received old papers about his father’s affairs in 1867 and destroyed them in 1871. It also quotes later family correspondence describing substantial trading debts paid by relatives. These are family-transmitted accounts, not independently inspected business records, but they help explain why the address alone cannot establish the size, use or ownership of his Bread Street premises.

timeline.text: Johnstone’s commercial guide describes Bread Street, Cheapside as containing 68 houses and records a cluster of trade and warehouse businesses. The transcription reviewed does not independently identify No. 7 with William Loyd.

name: Albyns Manor
summary: Albyns Manor was a Jacobean country house near Stapleford Abbotts; the mansion was demolished in 1955, while its former service range survives as a listed house.
connection: The workbook places Frederic Edward Loyd and his son Lewis at Albyns, but gives a move there after 1924; a 1902 directory instead records a Frederic E. Loyd in residence, leaving identity and dates unresolved.
status: The principal mansion was demolished in 1955. A former early 17th-century service range, converted to a house in the 20th century, survives and is Grade II listed.

paragraphs.heading: Identity and family evidence
paragraphs.text: Albyns Manor was in Stapleford Abbotts, Essex, rather than Romford proper. A 1902 directory transcription calls it Sir William Abdy's seat and property and lists Frederic E. Loyd as occupant. The workbook says Frederic moved there after 1924, so the dates and identity need more evidence.

paragraphs.heading: Surviving fabric
paragraphs.text: Historic England dates the surviving former service range to the early seventeenth century, records its twentieth-century conversion to a house, and says the main mansion was demolished in 1955. It is not the mansion itself.

paragraphs.heading: Estate papers and material survival
paragraphs.text: Essex Archives’ catalogue for the Abdy records names a 1925 illustrated sale catalogue of the Albyns estate, a 1926 estate plan and estate accounts. The catalogue is evidence that these documents survive, but their contents and sale result have not been inspected. Historic England separately records the mansion’s 1955 demolition and reused interior material in the former service range. Historic England’s archival image record EX00051A is a 1958 photographic copy of a plan, not a photograph of the house.

paragraphs.heading: Estate papers and material survival
paragraphs.text: The 1925 catalogue record’s scope is wider than the Albyns mansion: it groups Albyns with named Essex manors and farms, including Mascalls Bury, Abbots Hall, Barn Hall, Abbots Wick and Garnons Hall, and notes an illustrated Albyns sale catalogue, a 1926 plan and estate accounts. This describes the archive’s contents only; the sale catalogue, plan and accounts remain uninspected, so it does not establish what was sold or to whom.

paragraphs.heading: Photographs of surviving estate buildings
paragraphs.text: Photographs taken in 2012 show the former coach house and old manor wall at Albyns. They provide visual evidence of estate structures that survived the main mansion’s demolition in 1955; neither photograph shows the former main house.

timeline.text: A directory transcription lists Frederic E. Loyd as occupant of Albyns, while naming Sir William Abdy as owner.

name: Ballogie Estate
summary: Ballogie is a family-run rural estate in Royal Deeside; its present Ballogie House is a 1982–83 replacement on the site of the nineteenth-century mansion.
connection: The family workbook records a marriage into the Nicol family, John Wilmot Warner’s inheritance of Ballogie in 1941 and a later estate-management connection.
status: The estate website offers Ballogie House as holiday accommodation and a wedding venue, alongside farming, forestry and recreation. The present house is the 1982–83 replacement recorded by Aberdeenshire HER; the estate reports Nicol family stewardship since 1850.

paragraphs.heading: Estate and present activity
paragraphs.text: The estate’s official history describes a working rural business with farming, forestry, hospitality and recreation; its accommodation page currently offers Ballogie House for stays and weddings. The Nicol family says its stewardship began in 1850 and ownership passed to three family members in 2021.

paragraphs.heading: Earlier estate history
paragraphs.text: Historic Environment Scotland records the estate as Tillysnaught in 1650, belonging to the Roses of Kilravock. It subsequently passed through the Forbes, Innes and Farquharson families before James Dyce Nicol bought it in 1850. The surviving policies sundial is dated 1755, preserving evidence of the grounds before Nicol’s Victorian rebuilding. This sequence comes from the heritage record rather than inspected title deeds.

paragraphs.heading: Historic buildings and cultural landscape
paragraphs.text: The estate identifies Balnacraig House as a late-seventeenth-century laird’s house and notes the Donald Dinnie Stones and wartime Home Guard trench.

paragraphs.heading: Ballogie House sequence
paragraphs.text: Aberdeenshire HER says the present Ballogie House was built in 1982–83 on the site of its predecessor, a mansion built in 1852–55 for James Dyce Nicol and extended in 1885. HES’s separate sundial listing says Nicol built the predecessor in 1854 to designs by James Matthews and that it was later demolished; “now demolished” does not describe the present house.

paragraphs.heading: Connections through the wider family
paragraphs.text: The workbook records a marriage to James Dyce Nicol in 1844 and says John Wilmot Warner changed his surname to Nicol on inheriting Ballogie in November 1941. It also records Malcolm as an estate manager. These are distinct family connections through marriage, inheritance and employment, rather than evidence of ownership by someone bearing the Loyd surname. The inheritance detail is family-source evidence: no 1941 probate or conveyance has been inspected. The estate’s own account independently describes continuing Nicol family ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Ballogie heir and postwar occupation
paragraphs.text: A later biographical account of John Wilmot Warner Nicol says he became the fourth laird of Ballogie on his uncle’s death in 1941 and returned to the estate after the war. This independently supports the succession and residence sequence at a broad level, but does not verify the workbook’s exact November date or surname change from a probate or title record.

paragraphs.heading: Predecessor house in archive photographs
paragraphs.text: The Canmore photo series, dated 11 August 1981, documents the predecessor mansion before replacement: exterior elevations, portico, entrance hall and staircase, apartment interiors and cornice details. The catalogue credits RCAHMS; the views concern the demolished mansion, not today’s house.

paragraphs.heading: Ballogie House today
paragraphs.text: The estate’s Ballogie House accommodation gallery shows the replacement house, its rooms, garden and Deeside setting. This is the present house, not a view of the earlier mansion that was demolished before its 1982–83 replacement. The gallery does not date individual photographs.

paragraphs.heading: Family record
paragraphs.text: The 1840 Llandingat tithe apportionment scan directly lists Blaenos parcels 393–396 and 722–733 under David Jones, with the occupier entered as “Himself”; plot 393 is “House & Garden.” In the same schedule, a separate Garth issa House & Garden (plot 734) is also entered under Jones, while Garth ucha is listed separately under Revd R. Goddard with James Rees as occupier. The map scan locates these parcels in the parish. This establishes a Blaenos holding and nearby distinct Garth names by 1840, but does not prove that either was the “Blaenos estate” or Garth Farm in the later family record.

name: Coldham estate
summary: Victorian evidence identifies Lord Overstone as Coldham’s principal landowner. The workbook also places Lewis Vivian Loyd at Coldham, although his exact residence remains unidentified.
connection: The workbook records Lewis Loyd at Coldham; an 1879 directory independently identifies Lord Overstone as the principal landowner.
status: A substantial agricultural estate survives under the Coldham name. The exact Loyd residence and continuity of estate boundaries remain unresolved.

paragraphs.heading: The family connection
paragraphs.text: The workbook places Lewis Loyd at Coldham, Cambridgeshire. The 1879 Post Office Directory independently names Lord Overstone as the district’s principal landowner, but lists Herbert John Little at Coldham Hall. It therefore supports a family landholding connection without identifying Lewis’s house or proving that the Hall was his residence. The directory describes the recently formed ecclesiastical parish and its agricultural economy; its parish acreage must not be treated as estate acreage.

paragraphs.heading: Before the Loyds
paragraphs.text: The March Society’s local history traces the manor through the Peyton family and, citing William Watson’s 1827 history, reports that an earlier Coldham House was demolished around 1793 and replaced by a farmhouse. It reproduces details from an 1860 newspaper sale advertisement for an estate offered as 2,245 acres in five farms. An advertised auction is evidence of an offer, not proof of the eventual purchaser or completion.

paragraphs.heading: A much older landscape
paragraphs.text: A 2002 archaeological assessment for proposed wind turbines near Coldham Hall Farm reviews a landscape with prehistoric finds, Roman settlement and salt-making, and later drainage and reclamation. Its records include Roman pottery and corn-drying ovens discovered in 1933. These are findings about the surrounding estate landscape, not evidence that a particular Loyd house occupies a Roman building. The assessment also identifies nineteenth-century tithe mapping and earlier estate surveys.

paragraphs.heading: The estate in more recent records
paragraphs.text: Bidwells’ published sale account describes a 4,179-acre Coldham Estate, predominantly Grade 1 arable land, with grain and potato storage, residential property and income from wind and solar generation. It reports a sale above the £43.5 million guide. The account is undated, so no completion year is assigned here; its modern extent should not be assumed to match the Victorian holding.

paragraphs.heading: Before the Loyds
paragraphs.text: The March Society’s local-history account reproduces the 1860 sale notice’s five-farm schedule: Coldham Farm (660 acres), Stags Holt (505), Maltmas House (340), Friday Bridge (300) and Coldham Road (320), totalling the advertised 2,245 acres. The underlying Cambridge Chronicle advertisement is cited as 19 May 1860, page 5, but was not inspected here; the particulars describe an offer, not a completed sale or a proven Loyd acquisition.

paragraphs.heading: Additional archive records
paragraphs.text: Archive catalogue descriptions also record: Camille Silvy’s albumen photograph of Lewis Vivian Loyd (1852–1908), later associated with Coldham in the family record. This is a studio portrait made in London, not a photograph at the estate.

name: Coombe House (now Geoffrey Harris House)
summary: An 18th-century house on the Coombe estate, known today as Geoffrey Harris House and associated with Edward Loyd and his son Frank.
connection: The family workbook says Edward Loyd (1780–1863) lived at Coombe House; Croydon Council independently identifies Edward Lloyd as a tenant and says his son Frank owned it from 1892.
status: Grade II listed; historical uses include school and residential care home. Current use unverified.

paragraphs.heading: House and family association
paragraphs.text: Croydon's local landscape record says the house was built after 1761, let after 1833 and occupied by Edward Lloyd before his death in 1863. His son Frank owned it from 1892 and lived there until 1927; the family later gave adjoining land for Lloyd Park. This is the Croydon Coombe House, also called Geoffrey Harris House.

paragraphs.heading: Present status
paragraphs.text: The house and grounds are recorded in local heritage inventories. The London Parks & Gardens Trust notes former convalescent-home, school and residential-care uses; its detailed research was last updated in 2008, so present occupancy is not established.

paragraphs.heading: Gardens and changing uses
paragraphs.text: The gardens inventory identifies an eighteenth-century ice house, ornamental trees and former kitchen gardens, and cites 1892 sale particulars and a 1914 visit. It records St Margaret's School (1946–1985), later care use, and adoption of the Geoffrey Harris name in 1988. These historical entries do not prove current occupancy.

paragraphs.heading: Sale and vacancy evidence
paragraphs.text: A 2025 marketing particulars pack for the former Oakwood School site identifies Coombe House as a Grade II listed main building and states that the school had vacated in 2023 and that the building was vacant at the time of marketing. A 2025 local news report says a buyer had been found for the site but did not identify the buyer. These are dated marketing and press records; they do not establish the outcome of the sale, present ownership, or use after marketing.

paragraphs.heading: Gardens and changing uses
paragraphs.text: Historic England’s Images of England archive records the Georgian ice house in the grounds of Geoffrey Harris House, photographed on 27 June 2007. This documents surviving garden fabric at the Croydon Coombe House site; it does not establish present access or use.

paragraphs.heading: Photographs in the sale listing
paragraphs.text: Knight Frank’s listing gallery shows the principal Coombe House elevation, timbered stair hall, chapel and decorated period rooms. The listing identifies the Grade II house by its former name, Geoffrey Harris House; these images document the marketed site, though their exact photograph dates are not stated.

paragraphs.heading: The farm is not yet located
paragraphs.text: The workbook names Cowarth Park Farm in Sunningdale but gives no street address or tenure. Historic England lists Coworth Park Farmhouse on Church Lane as a Grade II house with a sixteenth-century core and later alterations. The spelling and locality make it a candidate, but the listing does not connect it to the Loyds. It is distinct from Coworth House, the mansion at the centre of the hotel estate.

paragraphs.heading: Cowarth Park in contemporary records
paragraphs.text: A 1871 London Gazette sheriff nomination describes John Alves Arbuthnot as “of Cowarth Park, Old Windsor”; a 1892 Gazette nomination describes Sir William Farmer as “of Cowarth Park, Sunningdale.” These contemporary records document the Cowarth spelling and named residents/associations at Cowarth Park, but neither identifies a farm or links the property to the Loyds. The Gazette wording is evidence of residence/style, not by itself proof of legal ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Different property: the Coworth Park mansion estate
paragraphs.text: Dorchester Collection's history for the separate Coworth House/mansion estate gives successive owners from Shepheard (1776) through Arbuthnots, William Farmer (1883), Lord Stanley (1899) and Galen Weston (1980s), then hotel opening in 2010. This operator account is not a title history of the Church Lane farmhouse. The Tank Museum separately confirms Vivian Loyd's engineering collaboration with John Carden; that context does not locate the farm.

paragraphs.heading: Listed farmhouse location and historic fabric
paragraphs.text: Historic England’s statutory entry gives Coworth Park Farmhouse’s National Grid Reference as SU 96171 68092 and describes a sixteenth-century timber-framed farmhouse, altered in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, now a house. This securely locates the listed farmhouse on Church Lane and describes its fabric. It remains only a candidate for the workbook’s Cowarth Park Farm: neither the spelling nor the listing ties Vivian or William Loyd to this building.

paragraphs.heading: Residence and reported transfer

paragraphs.heading: Historical identification
paragraphs.text: The family’s Greenhill is the Cheetham Hill residence, not Green Hill at Flixton or other places of the same name. Samuel Lewis’s 1848 topographical account names Green Hill as the seat of Edward Loyd, a Manchester banker. A University of Manchester study of the Loyd family describes their later country residence as Greenhill in Smedley Lane, Cheetham. The family workbook independently preserves the residence association, but does not supply a specific street number or tenure detail.

paragraphs.heading: Present trace
paragraphs.text: The site lies in a now-urban part of Manchester. The sources reviewed identify surviving Victorian houses and later development in Cheetham, but do not establish which modern plot corresponds to Greenhill itself. Current physical status is therefore unverified.

paragraphs.heading: A documented Loyd country residence
paragraphs.text: The University of Manchester study explicitly identifies Greenhill in Smedley Lane, Cheetham Hill as the Loyd family’s country residence and places Lewis Loyd’s childhood at the substantial house beside the family bank on King Street. This strengthens the identification of the family’s Greenhill and supplies the Smedley Lane locational clue, but gives no exact parcel, tenure instrument or demolition date for Greenhill itself.

The Victoria County History’s 2024 building study likewise places Haughton House c.1830 among Langston’s village patronage; its religious history says it likely served curates almost continuously until 1903, while noting a competing suggestion that William Dickson Carter briefly occupied it and that another local history attributes its construction to Carter. No architect is identified in these sources.

Historic England notes minor late-20th-century additions, including a second storey added to a formerly single-storey attached outbuilding. A West Oxfordshire 2014 planning schedule records permissions for alterations, extensions and a pool proposal; these records show applications/decisions, not verified completion.

name: Hesleyside Hall
summary: Hesleyside Hall is a Grade II* country house and historic seat of the Charlton family, with a Loyd family library association through William Loyd.
connection: The workbook says William Loyd established a library of Loyd books at Hesleyside; other entries record Loyd family links through the Charltons.
status: The estate supports visitor accommodation through Hesleyside Huts; this does not establish public access to, or present use of, the Hall itself.

paragraphs.heading: Historic house and grounds
paragraphs.text: Historic England describes Hesleyside as a country house centred on a fourteenth-century pele tower, expanded in the seventeenth century, with a south front dated 1719 and east wing altered by William Newton in 1796–1800. Its registered parkland covers 85 hectares. Historic England recorded the site as privately owned in 2000; this is not a current ownership check.

paragraphs.heading: Family connection
paragraphs.text: The family workbook says William Loyd established a library of Loyd books at Hesleyside, reportedly housing about 800 books collected by Reggie Loyd. Historic England and local heritage sources identify Hesleyside with the Charlton family. Parks & Gardens UK says the Hesleyside Papers remain in a private collection; that indicates a potential research lead, not access to or confirmation of the library contents. The documented family connection is therefore a library association, not Loyd ownership.

paragraphs.heading: The 1887 sale catalogue record
paragraphs.text: Historic England’s estate-sales catalogue indexes a volume dated 13 October 1887 for Hesleyside and lists the Hall, Garden House, Home Farm, stables, mill and numerous named farms across the district. This is evidence that a substantial group of properties was included in the sale-particulars volume; the catalogue view does not reveal lots, vendors, acreage, purchaser, or whether the Hall itself was offered or sold. It therefore cannot support a claim that the Charlton seat changed hands in 1887, nor resolve how the Loyd library came to be at Hesleyside.

paragraphs.heading: Present estate visitor use
paragraphs.text: The Hesleyside Huts operator lists Hesleyside Hall as its location and contact address, and offers accommodation in shepherd’s huts on the estate. This establishes current visitor accommodation associated with the estate while leaving the Hall’s own occupation and the Loyd book collection’s location unverified.

The south front dates from 1719.

name: Idaho
location: Ringwood area, historically Hampshire; Matchams area, Dorset
summary: Arthur Heneage Loyd (1868–1911, family number 50) lived at Idaho, a timber house near Ringwood.
connection: Arthur Heneage Loyd (1868–1911, family number 50) lived at Idaho, a timber house near Ringwood.
status: Historical identity is documented; the exact relationship between the original Idaho log house and the later demolished Matchams House needs further confirmation.

paragraphs.heading: An Oregon-pine landmark
paragraphs.text: Kelly’s 1898 Hampshire directory names Idaho as Captain Arthur Heneage Loyd’s seat and describes an Oregon-pine log mansion inspired by the Idaho State building at the Chicago Exposition. An illustrated contemporary account in The Studio (October 1898) independently names Arthur Loyd as the owner, depicts the actual house in E. W. Charlton’s drawing, and says he arranged with an American architect to obtain the wood and oversee work on site. The article describes a large ballroom, drawing room and balconies set within a pine forest. Neither source names that architect; the workbook’s Kirtland Cutter attribution still needs direct confirmation.

paragraphs.heading: Later site and uncertain fabric
paragraphs.text: Local parish history associates the Barnsfield Heath estate with a property later called Idaho and Matchams House. A Dorset Council consultation summary reports the parish council’s statement that Matchams House had been demolished and its site became Matchams Close. These sources do not establish whether Matchams House was the same building, a replacement, or a later phase of Idaho, so a single continuous building chronology cannot be asserted.

paragraphs.heading: A dated directory and a later construction account
paragraphs.text: The 1898 directory establishes that Idaho existed by that year and names Arthur Heneage Loyd. A later U.S. National Register nomination for the C. C. Koerner House says a replica of the Idaho State Building from the 1893 Chicago fair was built at Ringwood in 1896–97 and called Idaho. This institutionally hosted historical narrative supports the workbook’s broad date and design account, but is not a contemporary construction record. It does not name the English client or architect; the Kirtland Cutter attribution still needs direct evidence.

paragraphs.heading: Additional archive records
paragraphs.text: The Studio’s October 1898 “Studio-Talk: Ringwood” prints a full-house drawing by E. W. Charlton on page 53, captioned “The log-house ‘Idaho,’ near Ringwood”. Page 54 has further drawings of the front porch, fireplace, ballroom and drawing-room, with an account beginning on page 50. The earlier catalogue lead giving page 144 was incorrect; all cited pages were inspected in the full Internet Archive scan.

timeline.text: The NPS nomination’s historical narrative dates the Ringwood replica to 1896–97, broadly consistent with the workbook’s 1897 date. No contemporary construction record was inspected.
A digitised Ringwood directory describes Idaho as Captain Arthur Heneage Loyd’s Oregon-pine log mansion inspired by the Idaho State building at the Chicago Exposition.

Dorset Council’s consultation summary records the parish council’s account that Matchams House had been demolished and its site reused as Matchams Close; this does not establish the fate of original Idaho fabric.

name: Langleybury House and Estate
summary: Langleybury is an early eighteenth-century country house and estate associated with the Loyd family in the later nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
connection: The family workbook identifies William Jones Loyd as of Langleybury, records that his son Edward lived there, and notes burials at Langleybury.
status: The house is Grade II* listed and presently recorded by Historic England as a commercial property in fair condition with improving trend. Historic England names the site Langleybury House & Film Centre; details of day-to-day public use were not independently verified.

paragraphs.heading: House and estate
paragraphs.text: The early eighteenth-century Georgian house is associated with Robert Raymond, Lord Chief Justice. A 2024 Three Rivers committee report describes Victorian remodelling by William Jones Loyd around 1860–70 and extension by Edward Henry Loyd around 1890. Its estate group includes a stable block, cottages and an aisled barn.

paragraphs.heading: Loyd family association
paragraphs.text: The workbook places William Jones Loyd (1821–1885) at Langleybury, identifies Edward Henry Loyd as living there, and records family burials there. A local museum history independently reports that William Jones Loyd lived at Langleybury House and built St Paul’s Church in the parish in 1864. Residence and association are documented; this dossier does not infer a legal ownership chain from residence alone.

paragraphs.heading: Present status
paragraphs.text: Historic England records Langleybury House as Grade II*, in fair and improving condition, with commercial ownership; its site entry is titled Langleybury House & Film Centre. A recent council planning report also describes the historic parkland and listed ancillary buildings.

paragraphs.heading: Estate use and current project
paragraphs.text: The operator's public engagement site says the mansion has been used as a film location for about a decade and sets out proposals for education/commercial facilities around the historic farm group. These are operator statements and proposals, not evidence the works are complete or visitor access is unrestricted.

paragraphs.heading: Building phases and proposed reuse
paragraphs.text: The 2023 Three Rivers planning report reproduces Historic England’s assessment that the c.1725–28 Georgian house was remodelled for W.J. Loyd around 1860–70 and extended for E.H. Loyd around 1890. It also describes the nearby stable block, old farm cottages and aisled barn as part of the designated estate group, and records the house on the Heritage at Risk Register at that time. The application proposed a film hub, including filming and training facilities and changes to the house and ancillary buildings. This is planning evidence of a proposal and the site’s then filming use, not confirmation that the full scheme was built or that the house now operates as proposed.

paragraphs.heading: Present status
paragraphs.text: Historic England’s Images of England record includes a John Reeve photograph of Langleybury House & Film Centre made on 16 July 2000. The archival record independently anchors the named mansion’s appearance at that date; it says nothing about current operation or unrestricted public access.

paragraphs.heading: Contemporary directory account
paragraphs.text: The digitised 1898 Kelly’s directory identifies Langleybury as Edward Henry Loyd’s seat, gives the park as 220 acres and lists him among the principal landowners. It calls the brick mansion the seat of E.H. Loyd, says Robert Raymond erected it in 1729 and that it had since been considerably enlarged. The acreage describes parkland, not the estate’s legal extent.

paragraphs.heading: Photographic records and reuse limits
paragraphs.text: Historic England identifies an exact-house John Reeve photograph dated 16 July 2000 and a separate RCHME photographic job from 1976; the latter image service was unavailable when checked. A private photographic archive lists a vintage print under the exact title “Langleybury Hall” and sells reproduction prints, but provides no open licence. The British Library catalogues two 1833 Langleybury views, though it does not identify their subjects and the sheets are not digitised.

paragraphs.heading: A Sandringham estate service house
paragraphs.text: The family workbook places Sir Julian Loyd at Laycocks, Sandringham, before his later home at Perrystone Cottage. paragraphs.heading: Planning record and recurring estate employment
paragraphs.text: The 1987 planning decision names “Mr J Loyd, Laycocks, Sandringham” as applicant for a garage and oil-tank relocation at a separate site in Burnham Market. It confirms a person using the Laycocks address by 1987, but does not establish that the applicant was Sir Julian or that he owned Laycocks. Dersingham Village Voice No. 125 recalls Ken Martins working at Laycocks for Captain Fellows before the Second World War, independently reinforcing its role as land-agent accommodation.

paragraphs.heading: Family residence
paragraphs.text: The family record places Frank Loyd at Lealands House and says his son Alfred also lived there. A local history database independently transcribes Frank and Frances Loyd at Lealands House in the 1911 census. This supports historical residence, but not ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Building identification caution
paragraphs.text: Historic England lists Lealands Farmhouse in Groombridge/Withyham as a Grade II house with a probable seventeenth-century south wing and eighteenth-century remainder. paragraphs.heading: Identifying the correct Groombridge house
paragraphs.text: A recent archaeological assessment distinguishes the seventeenth-century Lealands House from the separate Lealands Farm recorded south of Groombridge Hill. The Weald’s 1911 census transcription places retired Lieutenant-Colonel Frank Kirkman Loyd and Frances at Lealands House, Groombridge, with servants in the household. This supports residence in the house named by the workbook; it does not make the nearby Grade II Lealands Farmhouse the same building or establish Loyd ownership. The assessment attributes eighteenth-century estate restoration to William Camfield and mid-nineteenth-century garden replanting to John Saint, part of the wider Groombridge estate history.

paragraphs.heading: Earlier house and Loyd building campaign
paragraphs.text: Kent HER says Edward Loyd bought the earlier Chittenden house in 1853, demolished it, and built the present mansion in 1855; its condition observations date from 2009.

paragraphs.heading: Family workbook evidence
paragraphs.text: The workbook places Edward and Llewellyn at Lillesden and reports wartime Red Cross use; the latter claim remains uncorroborated.

paragraphs.heading: Institutional uses
paragraphs.text: Kent HER records St Wilfrid’s school acquisition in 1922, the later separate sale of ancillary structures as the estate was broken up, and the girls’ school departure in 1998.

paragraphs.heading: Conversion and present status
paragraphs.text: The 2009 HER entry says the apartment-conversion application was still under consideration. The project architect later describes the conversion, and current sale marketing advertises 14 apartments; completion dates for individual phases remain unverified. A CC BY 2.0 photograph by dxa5on records the former house as Lillesden School on 31 October 2010, before restoration; it should not be mistaken for the present apartments.

paragraphs.heading: Estate architecture and setting
paragraphs.text: The Kent landscape study records the designed grounds; it dates the gate lodge and stable courtyard to about 1855 and notes later school use of the courtyard. These ancillary buildings formed part of the estate setting, not the main house.

paragraphs.heading: Inheritance and the surviving estate record
paragraphs.text: Kent HER’s landscape-history synthesis says Edward bought Lillesden in 1853 and died in 1890; after his widow died in 1900, the 199-hectare estate passed to youngest son Llewellyn. It says the estate was broken up in 1922: St Wilfrid’s acquired the house with about 10 hectares, while the lodge, stable, kitchen garden and water tower were sold separately when the property was later acquired for development. Historic England Archive also catalogues the 23 June 1913 sale particulars as volume SC00558, covering the house and estate properties; the particulars themselves have not been inspected, so their lots and outcome remain unknown.

paragraphs.heading: The restored house today
paragraphs.text: The Ashton Stripp sales gallery shows the mansion after renovation: restored brick elevations, a shared entrance hall, an arched staircase and modern apartment interiors. The marketed two-bedroom apartment retains tall windows and ceiling decoration alongside a contemporary kitchen and bathrooms. Grounds photographs show lawns, mature trees, terrace steps and the approach. These are marketing photographs of the residential conversion, not evidence of the rooms’ appearance during Loyd occupation. The agent describes approximately 26 acres of shared grounds; this is an advertised figure rather than a verified title boundary. Photograph dates are not supplied, and the gallery does not establish present ownership or availability.

name: Lockinge House and Estate
location: East Lockinge, near Wantage, Oxfordshire, England (historic county of Berkshire)
summary: Lockinge House was the Loyd-Lindsay family’s country seat within the wider Lockinge estate; the house was demolished in 1947, while the estate remains an active rural and property enterprise.
connection: The family workbook links Harriet Sarah Loyd-Lindsay (Lady Wantage) and her husband Robert to Lockinge House, records Arthur Thomas Loyd as living there, and notes the Lockinge burials of Harriet Wright and Lord Overstone.
status: Lockinge House was demolished in 1947. The Lockinge Estate continues to operate across farmland, woodland and let residential and commercial properties; its website reports about 6,000 acres, 150 homes and 60 commercial units. The historic orangery at Lockinge Stables survives as a Grade II listed building.

paragraphs.heading: The house and the wider estate
paragraphs.text: Lockinge House stood at East Lockinge near Wantage, separate from the wider estate. Published dates for its core differ: the Vale & Downland Museum gives 1730, Royal Berkshire History about 1750, and the family workbook 1773. The surviving orangery at the former stables is a distinct building, dated by Historic England to about 1730.

paragraphs.heading: Loyd-Lindsay ownership
paragraphs.text: The Lockinge Estate says its formation and expansion took place between 1854 and 1890, after Harriet Loyd and Robert James Lindsay received the manor at East Lockinge on marriage and acquired further land. The National Gallery’s catalogue says Lewis Loyd acquired the estate in 1854 and his son, Lord Overstone, settled it on Harriet and Robert at their marriage in 1858. The workbook also calls the house a wedding gift. Village relocation and estate works later reshaped the setting.

paragraphs.heading: Life at Lockinge in the family memoir
paragraphs.text: The 1907 memoir by Harriet, Lady Wantage, recalls that Lockinge became the couple’s home after their 1858 marriage; it describes later house enlargements celebrated in 1869 and the house as a base for military visitors and manoeuvres on the Berkshire Downs. This is a participant’s retrospective account, not a building plan or military log.

paragraphs.heading: The picture collection at Lockinge
paragraphs.text: A 1905 picture catalogue locates the household’s tapestry hall and many English paintings at Lockinge, while family portraits and other pictures were kept at Overstone. The catalogue was compiled at Lord Wantage’s request from an earlier 1875 inventory and records the contents and room associations of the family collection; it is direct evidence of the house’s cultural use, not a plan of its architecture.

paragraphs.heading: Designed gardens and the rocky stream
paragraphs.text: The Pulham Legacy identifies two circa 1910 photographs of the rocky stream at Lockinge, reproduced with Thomas Loyd's permission. They document the designed gardens created by James Pulham & Son in the 1860s, separate from the demolished main house.

paragraphs.heading: Historic photographs of the demolished house
paragraphs.text: The Vale & Downland Museum publishes Tom Reveley’s view of the house and church around 1900, with the lake in the foreground. Two reproductions in Royal Berkshire History show the mansion’s entrance elevation and a coloured view of the conservatory and waterside grounds. The DiCamillo collection adds a postcard dated about 1920. Together these images document the lost main house, rather than the surviving orangery. Historic England’s north-west photograph remains a useful catalogue reference, but its image service was unavailable during this review.

paragraphs.heading: Estate life and demolition
paragraphs.text: The estate's obituary describes Lockinge House as a large family home requiring fifty servants and says Christopher Loyd chose its demolition amid post-war staffing and financial pressures. Demolition began in 1947 and the family moved to Betterton. This is estate-authored recollection, not a demolition file.

paragraphs.heading: Demolition and surviving fabric
paragraphs.text: After Arthur Thomas Loyd died in 1944, Lockinge House was demolished in 1947. The National Gallery independently places demolition a few years after his death. The house is gone; Historic England's Grade II orangery and converted commercial estate buildings are separate survivors.

paragraphs.heading: Present estate
paragraphs.text: The estate website describes today's Lockinge and Ardington operation as farmland, woodland, housing and commercial property; it reports around 150 residential properties and 60 commercial units, most let. This is the wider estate, not a surviving Lockinge House.

paragraphs.heading: Wider estate in photographs
paragraphs.text: The estate’s own contemporary galleries show surviving village cottages, converted farm and commercial buildings, lanes, garden areas and grazing land. These views document the continuing estate landscape and enterprise; none depicts Lockinge House, which was demolished in 1947. The website does not give individual photograph dates or precise locations for every view.

timeline.text: According to the National Gallery’s catalogue, Lewis Loyd acquired the estate in 1854; Lord Overstone settled it on Harriet and Robert at their 1858 marriage.
Estate formation and village changes followed, according to the Lockinge Estate history.
Arthur Thomas Loyd died in 1944; Lockinge House was demolished in 1947.
Historic England dates the surviving stable orangery to about 1730; it is not the main house.
Berkshire history gives c.1750 for Lockinge House; the workbook says 1773, so its exact construction date remains uncertain.
Christopher Loyd is credited with choosing demolition; the family moved to Betterton.
The estate website reports about 6,000 acres, 150 homes and 60 commercial units.

paragraphs.heading: The listed Middleton Cheney house
paragraphs.text: Historic England lists Middleton House as Grade II, with seventeenth- or eighteenth-century origins and a 1801 refronting; its datestone reads 1638 and 1801. It describes a brick front, older limestone sides and rear, and early nineteenth-century interior work. Parish sources place it in the Manor Farm area shown on old maps. This is Middleton Cheney in Northamptonshire, not every house of that name.

paragraphs.heading: Associated family entry
paragraphs.text: The workbook associates James Henry (“Jimmy”) Lane Fox with Middleton House. A separate genealogical entry identifies the same James Henry Lane Fox, gives his marriage to Anne Loyd in 1937, and records that he lived at Middleton House, Middleton Cheney, citing Burke’s Peerage (1999). This independently supports the residence association, though it does not establish a title transfer or exact occupation dates.

name: Minshull Vernon estate
summary: Minshull Vernon is a Cheshire parish and historic manor-landscape; the family workbook associates an estate here with Edward Henry Loyd, while Newfield Hall is a distinct Grade II-listed house within the parish.
connection: The family workbook says Edward Henry Loyd inherited the Minshull Vernon estate from Lewis; historical directories identify Edward Henry Loyd as a major landowner and owner of Newfield Hall in the township.
status: The civil parish remains rural; Newfield Hall is extant and Grade II listed. Current ownership or operation of the wider historic estate is unverified.

paragraphs.heading: Estate and buildings
paragraphs.text: This dossier concerns a place/estate association, not one mansion. Historic England identifies Newfield Hall, Middlewich Road, as an early nineteenth-century brick mansion with an earlier farmhouse attached. Kelly's 1896 directory calls Edward Henry Loyd owner of Newfield Hall, lord of the manor and a principal landowner. A 1891 will report leaves Lewis Loyd's Cheshire property to his nephew, but does not specify Newfield Hall alone.

paragraphs.heading: Manor, estate and Newfield Hall
paragraphs.text: The Kelly directory identifies Edward Henry Loyd as lord of the manor and principal owner and names Newfield Hall as his property. Historic England describes an earlier altered farmhouse attached behind the mansion. A separate 1848 purchase/1849 demolition concerns old Minshull Hall, not Newfield Hall. A railway archive catalogue also lists an agreement with Lewis Loyd for land at Minshull Vernon; the item and parcel were not examined.

paragraphs.heading: Manor ownership and railway land sale
paragraphs.text: The 1870–72 Imperial Gazetteer says the manor, with Norfield and Erdswick Halls, then belonged to Lewis Loyd. Separately, the LNWR Society catalogue lists AGR0052 as an extract from an agreement dated 28 April 1887 for the railway’s purchase of land from Lewis Loyd at Minshull Vernon. The first is a printed gazetteer and the second a catalogue description; neither parcel map nor agreement text was examined, so the railway strip cannot yet be located or treated as the whole estate.

paragraphs.heading: Estate and mansion

paragraphs.heading: Estate boundaries and archive evidence

The record dates institutional mapping of redevelopment on the former estate, but the plan was not inspected and does not define the Loyd mansion’s footprint.

name: Overstone Hall (Overstone Park)
summary: Overstone Hall is a Grade II listed Victorian country house within the historic Overstone Park estate, built in the 1860s for Samuel Jones-Loyd and Harriet, Lady Overstone, and now awaiting an unresolved restoration and enabling-development process.
connection: The Loyd family workbook links the estate first to Lewis Loyd (1768–1858), then to his son Samuel Jones-Loyd, Lady Wantage, and later Lewis Vivian Loyd; several detailed inheritance and sale claims in that entry remain uncorroborated by the public heritage sources reviewed.
status: The main house remains a fire-damaged listed building. On 2 July 2026 the council committee resolved to delegate authority to grant the Hall restoration/conversion applications, subject to requirements; the separate 77-home enabling scheme was deferred. Issued final permissions and completed works have not been established.

paragraphs.heading: The earlier estate and Victorian house
paragraphs.text: Historic England lists Overstone College (the house commonly called Overstone Hall) as a mid-19th-century country house designed by W. M. Teulon for the first Lord Overstone. The separate architectural study by Megan Leyland says Lewis Loyd bought the earlier estate from John Kipling and that the 1860–64 house replaced an earlier mansion.

paragraphs.heading: Loyd family connection
paragraphs.text: Samuel Jones-Loyd, later first Baron Overstone, commissioned the Victorian house. The parish history attributes the building campaign to Lady Overstone's wish. The workbook links the later estate to Samuel, his daughter Harriet (Lady Wantage), and Lewis Vivian Loyd. Independent estate research says Lady Wantage's nephew inherited the remaining estate in 1920 and the estate was marketed in 1921 after Sir Harry Mallaby-Deeley directed a sale under an assignment held as security. This supports a sale process, not the workbook's wording that Lewis Vivian personally sold the interest; the family may conflate him with his son and heir, Lewis Richard William Loyd.

paragraphs.heading: Present condition and proposals
paragraphs.text: Historic England records extensive damage from a 2001 fire. A separate 2023 fire further damaged the derelict Hall; investigators said it was started deliberately. On 2 July 2026, the committee resolved to delegate authority to grant restoration of part of the Hall and apartment conversion, subject to requirements; it deferred the separate 77-home proposal for more information. These are planning outcomes, not evidence of completed work.

paragraphs.heading: Archival trail and estate records
paragraphs.text: The National Archives directory identifies the Loyd family and Barons Overstone papers at Northamptonshire Archives (NRA 4952); this catalogue entry is a research lead, not evidence that individual deeds/accounts were examined. The University of Reading says Lord Overstone's private library was kept at Overstone Park until Lady Wantage bequeathed it in 1920.

paragraphs.heading: Archaeological work and committee outcomes
paragraphs.text: The Northamptonshire HER summarizes an interim evaluation after December 2025 trial trenching, noting possible remains associated with the early Hall and trackway; it said a final report would follow further work. July 2026 minutes record a delegated-grant resolution on the listed-building application and deferral of the enabling-housing proposal. Neither confirms that restoration has begun.

paragraphs.heading: Archival trail and estate records
paragraphs.text: The family’s 1905 picture catalogue places portraits of Samuel Jones Loyd and Harriet Overstone with their daughter Harriet Sarah at Overstone, while the 1907 memoir says the house was built under Lady Overstone’s supervision as her intended home. These are direct family-era accounts of the household and use; they do not document title or the later estate sale.

paragraphs.heading: Contemporary architectural image
paragraphs.text: The Builder’s 1 March 1862 issue included an elevation and ground plan of Overstone Hall, identified in an architectural study as William Milford Teulon’s design. This contemporary engraving records the intended building, not a photograph or proof that every detail was completed. The published 1862 illustration is public domain; a usable digital reproduction is not available from the linked record.

paragraphs.heading: The damaged hall in a developer photograph
paragraphs.text: A Fairline Homes project page includes an aerial photograph of the surviving, fire-damaged Overstone Hall and its park setting. The image is undated and does not itself establish the current stage or outcome of any restoration proposal.

paragraphs.heading: A contemporary family notice
paragraphs.text: The 1921 Hertford College Magazine announces Major Charles Micklem’s marriage to Diana Gertrude May, daughter of Mr and Mrs Graham Loyd of Ovington House, Ovington Gardens. A 1914 London court directory lists William Graham Loyd at 1A Ovington Square; the relationship between those address descriptions is not established here.

paragraphs.heading: Avoiding a namesake
paragraphs.text: The workbook locates this residence in London. Accounts of Ovington House in Hampshire concern a different property and should not be used to describe the Loyd home.

paragraphs.heading: The Victorian neighbourhood
paragraphs.text: The garden’s own historical account dates the development of Ovington Square to 1844, on Elizabeth, Baroness von Zandt’s estate, with architect W. W. Pocock. It explains that the London square took its name from the family’s earlier Hampshire home. This gives useful context for the London address without transferring the history of the Hampshire house to the Loyds. The precise relationship between Ovington House, Ovington Gardens and the directory’s 1A Ovington Square still needs a contemporary plan or numbered rate-book entry.

paragraphs.text: Local map-focused history says a large house called Kersal Mount was present by the 1845 map and had become Prestwich Lodge by 1891. Parks & Gardens UK, citing the 1994 Greater Manchester historic parks survey, says parts survive and it is the golf-club clubhouse. paragraphs.heading: Survival and present use
paragraphs.text: The Parks & Gardens UK inventory describes the principal house as surviving in part and functioning as the golf course clubhouse, with much of the former grounds absorbed into the golf course. Its inventory cites a 1994 historic parks survey, so the use statement is not a fresh 2026 operator confirmation. This is the historic private residence, not Prestwich’s separate former asylum site.

paragraphs.heading: Former vicarage at Ocle Pychard
paragraphs.text: Herefordshire HER indexes Remenham House as a former vicarage. Its source index establishes the existence of an HER record, not the contents of the underlying record unless separately read. An archived Knight Frank brochure describes Remenham House and Vicarage Cottage as separate properties and characterizes the house as a substantial red-brick dwelling with slate roof and period detailing. paragraphs.heading: Recent residential use evidence
paragraphs.text: Herefordshire Council’s planning search records application P233719/FH at Remenham House for a domestic outbuilding with garage, storage and gymnasium. summary: Shaw Hill House was a country house associated with Frederic Edward Loyd and his family; the principal house was demolished in the 1960s and its site is now developed and community open space.

paragraphs.heading: The demolished country house at Shaw
paragraphs.text: This is Shaw Hill House in Shaw near Melksham, not the separate Shaw House. The workbook associates Frederic Edward Loyd and his son Lewis with it. The parish history says the house existed before 1825. Melksham Times Past identifies Rev. Thomas Heathcote and son Thomas Jenkyns Heathcote as residents, then Charles Awdry c.1890–1908; these occupancies do not independently corroborate the Loyds.

paragraphs.heading: School use and loss
paragraphs.text: Melksham Times Past reports Beltane School’s country branch moved to Shaw Hill in December 1939. Parish history says the house was used during the war, was demolished around 1965, and The Beeches was built in 1968. Historic England’s Folly Lane listing links a surviving cottage to the estate but gives a conflicting demolition chronology, so the exact date remains unresolved.

name: Spencer House
summary: A wartime military roll places the Loyd family’s Spencer House on Wendover Road, correcting an earlier mistaken association with a house in Whitchurch.
connection: The family workbook records Edward ‘Ted’ Loyd living at Spencer House, Aylesbury; it does not establish ownership.
status: The Wendover Road address is documented in a 1915 roll. The surviving Spenser House villa is a strong candidate, but continuity with the named family residence still needs documentary confirmation.

paragraphs.heading: The Loyd address in an original record
paragraphs.text: The family workbook places Captain Edward (“Ted”) Loyd at Spencer House, Aylesbury. An original Canadian Expeditionary Force nominal roll, issued in 1915 for Lord Strathcona’s Horse, supplies the missing street: the entry for Sergeant Edward B. K. Loyd, service number 2650, gives Captain E. K. Loyd as next of kin at Spencer House, Wendover Road, Aylesbury. This is direct period evidence for the address, rather than a match based only on a house name.

paragraphs.heading: An 1893 villa on the same road
paragraphs.text: Buckinghamshire’s Historic Environment Record identifies Byron, Milton and Spenser villas on Wendover Road as a group built in 1893. It describes three-storey houses in buff and red brick, half-hipped slate roofs, large chimney stacks, bay windows and ornate open porches. Spenser House’s near-identical name and the road match make it a strong candidate for the military-roll address; the different spelling and absence of a numbered address in that roll mean the identification remains qualified.

paragraphs.heading: The photographed building
paragraphs.text: The council’s conservation-area appraisal includes a labelled photograph of Spenser House on printed page 73, within its assessment of Wendover Road. This gives a specific image of the candidate villa, rather than the unrelated London mansion. The photograph remains linked to its original council document because no explicit reuse licence was verified.

paragraphs.heading: Correction of the earlier account
paragraphs.text: An earlier version of this page associated the family with Spencer House in Little London, Whitchurch. The council footpath file establishes that a house of that name exists there, but does not connect it to the Loyds. The period Wendover Road address is stronger evidence. Whitchurch’s modern sale and reported wartime history have therefore been removed from this account; neither belongs in the family house’s history without a proven connection.

timeline.text: Council heritage records date the Wendover Road group including Spenser House to 1893; its identification with the later Loyd address remains qualified.

The conservation-area appraisal names and photographs Spenser House among the key Wendover Road buildings.

name: Sprivers
summary: Sprivers is a historic Courthope house and park in Horsmonden, with roots in a medieval farmstead and a mid-eighteenth-century country mansion.
connection: The workbook identifies George Courthope as of Sprivers and records that his wife Elinor died there in 1895.
status: Agent marketing describes an operating wedding venue and advertises a new lease. A 2022 planning report records no public access at that time; current access, use and legal ownership are not independently verified.

paragraphs.heading: House and grounds
paragraphs.text: The National Trust dates Sprivers Park to the mid-eighteenth century, when Alexander Courthope made it the setting for a country mansion built onto Lower Sprivers’ medieval farmstead. Its record links the Courthopes to the iron industry and Horsmonden Furnace. This landscape record does not establish that the Trust owns or operates the house.

paragraphs.heading: Courthope and Loyd connection
paragraphs.text: The workbook identifies George Courthope as of Whiligh and Sprivers and records his wife Elinor’s residence at Whiligh and death at Sprivers in December 1895. This is family evidence of association, not proof of Loyd ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Land tenure and house development
paragraphs.text: A National Trust archaeological report summarises documentary references showing Lower and Upper Sprivers were once held separately and were reunited by John Courthope through purchases in 1700–1704. The Kent Compendium and statutory listing describe the surviving mansion as a fifteenth-century core, extended in the sixteenth century and altered and extended for Alexander Courthope in 1756. The workbook’s connection is later: Elinor Courthope died at Sprivers in 1895, while no independent evidence reviewed here demonstrates Loyd ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Present use and access
paragraphs.text: The 2022 neighbourhood-plan examination report says the main house at Sprivers was being used as a wedding venue and that the house and grounds had no public access; the examiner recommended excluding its curtilage from the proposed local green space. A current commercial listing also describes Sprivers Mansion as an operating wedding and events venue and advertises a lease opportunity, but this is agent marketing rather than a title record. The National Trust landscape record does not establish ownership of the mansion.

paragraphs.heading: Land tenure and house development
paragraphs.text: The inspected 2007 National Trust commissioned building survey concerns Nos. 1 and 2 Sprivers Cottages opposite the mansion, not the mansion itself. It records late-eighteenth-century cottages with brick lower floors, timber-framed upper storeys, bread ovens and an adjoining outbuilding; its map review found the site on a 1775 plan and earliest mapped evidence in 1840. The report cites a 1700 sale deed to John Courthope for £185 among the purchases that reunited Upper and Lower Sprivers by 1704; the underlying deeds were not inspected for this dossier.

paragraphs.heading: Additional archive records
paragraphs.text: Archive catalogue descriptions also record: Specific building record for the Grade II* mansion at Sprivers with five identification images, four credited to National Trust and Dr N. R. Bannister and one to the venue; reuse terms are not stated on the record.

paragraphs.heading: Venue rooms and garden photographs
paragraphs.text: The Sprivers Mansion venue galleries show the Georgian Blue and Yellow Rooms, entrance hall, garden and Rose Garden Wing. These views document the surviving house in its event and accommodation use. Individual photographs are not dated by the operator.

timeline.text: The workbook records Elinor Courthope’s death at Sprivers.
John Courthope acquired the separate Upper and Lower Sprivers holdings, according to the National Trust archaeological report’s cited deed references.
The house was altered and extended for Alexander Courthope.

name: The Oaks
summary: The Oaks is an early eighteenth-century country house now operating as the Royal Berkshire Hotel.
connection: Hannah Loyd (later Entwisle) was recorded in the family workbook as living at The Oaks in her widowhood; this establishes residence, not ownership.
status: The historic house operates as the Royal Berkshire Hotel; current hotel information identifies it as part of Exclusive Collection.

paragraphs.heading: The Oaks, later Little Paddocks
paragraphs.text: Local Berkshire history dates The Oaks to 1705, built for Charles Churchill and Lady Mary, and reports later residents Robert Blane (from 1846) and Mrs Entwistle (from 1880). It identifies Entwistle as Hannah Loyd and says she bought the house after her husband’s death, living there until 1907. This local-history account supports a long residence and reports a purchase, but no title record was inspected; the workbook independently associates Hannah with the house. Royal Berkshire Archives catalogues interior photographs from c.1915–20, when Colonel James Nockells Horlick owned it.

paragraphs.heading: Institutional and hotel use
paragraphs.text: The Berkshire history account says the house became Little Paddocks, housed the Barclay School for Partially Sighted Girls (1941–69), then became a hotel. The operator identifies the current business as the Royal Berkshire Hotel.

paragraphs.heading: The Oaks, later Little Paddocks
paragraphs.text: Royal Berkshire Archives lists an interior photograph of The Oaks (later Little Paddocks), reference D/EX2780/1/36, from about 1915–20 when Colonel James Nockells Horlick owned it. The archival photograph is later than Hannah Entwistle’s reported residence and cannot corroborate her purchase or occupancy.

paragraphs.heading: Additional archive records
paragraphs.text: Archive catalogue descriptions also record: Specific archival photograph of a room interior at The Oaks (later Little Paddocks), Sunninghill, circa 1915–20, while owned by Colonel (later Sir) James Nockells Horlick; reference D/EX2780/1/36. Archive says images are for information unless otherwise stated and reuse requires permission.

paragraphs.heading: The house as a hotel today
paragraphs.text: The Royal Berkshire operator’s gallery shows the surviving house exterior, period interior rooms, staircase and landscaped grounds. These photographs illustrate the historic house in its hotel use; the gallery gives no exact dates for individual images.

timeline.text: Royal Berkshire Archives holds photographs of the house interior. Room photograph D/EX2780/1/36 shows furniture, paintings and decorative details during Colonel James Nockells Horlick’s ownership.

name: Thornhill
location: Castle Hill, Cowes, Isle of Wight, England
summary: Thornhill was Edward Loyd’s Isle of Wight residence overlooking the Royal Yacht Squadron and is now a residential building divided into apartments.
connection: The family workbook identifies Thornhill as Edward Loyd’s Isle of Wight residence and says his son Llewellyn’s house there was converted into apartments.
status: Thornhill, Castle Hill, Cowes, is now divided into flats/apartments; Cowes Town Council considered works to its communal bike store and terrace in 2019. No listing record for the house itself was found.

paragraphs.heading: Loyd residence and Cowes setting
paragraphs.text: The workbook identifies Thornhill as Edward Loyd’s Isle of Wight residence, situated behind Holy Trinity Church and overlooking the Royal Yacht Squadron. A specialist architectural history of Lillesden notes Edward Loyd’s later transformation into a Kent landowner and Royal Yacht Squadron member at “Lillesden Kent and Thornhill, Cowes.” The Cowes Historic Environment Record search did not yield a dedicated entry for Thornhill, and its architectural history and construction date remain unverified.

paragraphs.heading: Apartment conversion and current use
paragraphs.text: The family workbook says Llewellyn Loyd’s house, Thornhill, had been converted into apartments. Cowes Town Council’s planning committee considered an application for “Thornhill, Castle Hill” in 2019 concerning a communal bike store and terrace. Current commercial property information independently locates multiple flats in the building at Castle Hill, confirming residential subdivision. No claim is made about present ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Yachting and the garden’s later history
paragraphs.text: The Victorian Society’s Manchester history identifies Thornhill as Edward Loyd’s summer residence. It records his yachts Gelert, launched at West Cowes in April 1867, and Daydream, owned in 1871–1876. It also reports that the Royal Yacht Squadron acquired Thornhill’s gardens in 1891 after his death, extending the Castle lawns. That account concerns the gardens: it should not be read as evidence that the whole house changed ownership at the same time.

timeline.text: Edward Loyd’s yacht Gelert launched at West Cowes.
Historical account reports acquisition of Thornhill’s gardens by the Royal Yacht Squadron.
Cowes Town Council considered alterations to the communal bike store and terrace at Thornhill, Castle Hill.

name: Threepwood, Haydon
summary: The family workbook uses both Threepwood Hall and Threepwood Farmhouse for John Michael Loyd’s residence. Separate listed buildings carry those names, so the exact building remains unresolved.
connection: Michael’s updated biography gives Threepwood Farmhouse; his daughters’ workbook entries give their father’s address as Threepwood Hall. Both descriptions place the family near Haydon Bridge.
status: Historic England lists Threepwood Hall and Threepwood Hall Farmhouse separately. The exact building occupied by the family, its current use and ownership are not established here.

paragraphs.heading: Two names in the family records
paragraphs.text: Michael’s updated biography calls his residence Threepwood Farmhouse. The workbook entries for his daughters Tessa, Chloe and Daisy instead name Threepwood Hall. The address descriptions cannot be resolved by preferring one worksheet: they might reflect a changed residence, local naming or inconsistent recording. Both forms are retained as family evidence; neither proves title or identifies a particular listed structure.

paragraphs.heading: Two separately listed buildings
paragraphs.text: Historic England’s Threepwood Hall entry describes late-seventeenth-century remodelling and late-eighteenth-century enlargement. Its separate Threepwood Hall Farmhouse entry describes an early-nineteenth-century house with squared stonework, slate roof and a symmetrical three-window front. The two statutory entries concern distinct buildings. A contemporary residence record or parcel-level match is needed before assigning either architectural history to the family home.

paragraphs.heading: Contemporary address evidence
paragraphs.text: The official 1992 Gazette notice appointing county High Sheriffs identifies John Michael Loyd as “of Threepwood Hall, Haydon Bridge, Hexham.” This independently confirms that “Threepwood Hall” was a contemporary address associated with him by 1992. It does not settle whether the family occupied the separately listed Hall or Hall Farmhouse, prove ownership, or show that he resided there throughout the period implied by the workbook.

paragraphs.heading: Two separately listed buildings
paragraphs.text: Historic England’s archive records distinguish the two properties in dated photographs by David Lumley: Threepwood Hall on 10 April 2002 (IOE01/06338/24) and Threepwood Hall Farmhouse on 8 April 2002 (IOE01/06338/14). The photos reinforce that these are separate structures, but their captions do not identify which one the Loyd family occupied.

name: Tormore House and Farm
location: Ardvasar, Sleat, Isle of Skye, Highland, Scotland
summary: Tormore is a historic farm and house in Sleat; local history documents nineteenth-century estate tenancy and a Loyd family's later tenancy, while current use of the house is unverified.
connection: The workbook records Evelyn Loyd living at Tormore; the local history society says her father F. E. Loyd rented the farm and Evelyn succeeded to the tenancy, not ownership.
status: The local history society reports that much of the old farm passed to the Forestry Commission in the 1960s and was later bought by the community trust; the current status of Tormore House is unverified.

paragraphs.heading: Farm and house history
paragraphs.text: The Highland HER cites Macdonald estate records for repairs to Tormore House in 1802–03, further improvements in 1829 and additions in 1892–93; these are catalogue descriptions, not records read directly. Sleat Local History Society reports the later farm tenancy of F. E. Loyd and his daughter Evelyn, rather than Loyd ownership. The 1883 Napier Commission transcript identifies the earlier farmer Donald Macdonald.

paragraphs.heading: Estate landscape and limits
paragraphs.text: The local history society reports that Lord Macdonald sold most farmland to the Forestry Commission in the 1960s and that a community trust later bought and restored woodland. It does not establish that Tormore House transferred with the farmland or document the house’s present use.

paragraphs.heading: Tenancy end bounded by gravestone evidence
paragraphs.text: An image transcription and photograph catalogue for Skye gravestones records Evelyn S. Loyd at Tormore with dates 17 April 1885–9 August 1962. The local history account says she continued the farm tenancy until her death in the 1960s; the memorial narrows her death to 1962 but does not prove when her tenancy began or whether the house passed with farmland later sold to Forestry Commission.

paragraphs.heading: Estate landscape and limits
paragraphs.text: Sleat Local History Society’s image gallery includes two unidentified historic scenes captioned “Stalkers at Tormore” and “Working with sheep at Tormore.” They document sporting and farm activity at the place, but neither the catalogue captions nor available identifications show F. E. Loyd or Evelyn Loyd.

name: Towersey Manor
summary: Peter Loyd (1923–1974, family number 99) is recorded in the workbook as living at Towersey Manor.
connection: Peter Loyd (1923–1974, family number 99) is recorded in the workbook as living at Towersey Manor.
status: Grade II listed manor house; the neighbourhood plan describes community events in its grounds. Current title ownership is unverified.

paragraphs.heading: A nineteenth-century manor house
paragraphs.text: The adopted Towersey neighbourhood plan says Edward Griffin built the present Italian-style manor house in 1858. J. Whitehouse Griffin sold it to Paulyn Rawdon Hastings in 1899; Hastings substantially rebuilt it before selling to G. J. C. Harter in 1911. Historic England instead dates the listed house probably to the early 19th century, with later 19th-century additions. Whether this difference reflects rebuilding or conflicting dating remains unresolved.

paragraphs.heading: Fabric and family connection
paragraphs.text: Historic England describes the listed house at 45 Manor Road as stone rubble with brick dressings, a hipped slate roof, later additions and decorative 19th-century plaster ceilings. The workbook records Peter Loyd as living at Towersey Manor, but provides no independently corroborated dates or ownership evidence. The neighbourhood plan mentions village fêtes and open-garden events in the grounds; these are historical references, not a current access schedule.

Historic England’s listing instead dates the original house probably to the early 19th century, with later 19th-century additions.
