name: Upper House
summary: Upper House was a residence associated with the Loyd family in the early twentieth century; its architectural history and current status are unverified.
connection: The family workbook records William Loyd living at Upper House; a local history account independently recalls William Brownlow Loyd hosting cricket matches there.
status: Current status unverified; no reliable source found confirming the present building or use.

paragraphs.heading: Farmhouse enlarged by Norman Shaw
paragraphs.text: Shamley Green’s 1993 village history says Upper House Lane’s Upper House began as a farm, was bought in 1874 by Ellinor Guthrie, and was redesigned and enlarged for her large family by architect Richard Norman Shaw. The account provides a stronger basis for the architectural attribution than the previously cited Lutyens Trust page, which concerns Chinthurst Hill and only references Shaw’s Upper House commission in passing. Archaeological research separately describes Upper House Farm as an originally 15th-century hall house; exact relationship between farm remnant and the later house needs care.

paragraphs.heading: Loyd-era association
paragraphs.text: The family workbook identifies William Brownlow Loyd with Upper House. Shamley Green local history records his cricket matches with Run Common, supporting local residence and social activity but not ownership. The building is also associated with the Guthrie family before the Loyd connection; no source reviewed establishes a title transfer to the Loyds or confirms continuity of the current building fabric.

paragraphs.heading: Photographic record
paragraphs.text: The 1993 village history reproduces a photograph captioned “Upper House 1988”, showing the large timber-framed house. It is a dated view of the named property, but does not establish the building’s present condition or use.

name: Whiligh Estate
location: Ticehurst and Wadhurst, East Sussex, England
summary: Whiligh is a historic Courthope estate centred on a Grade II* listed house in Ticehurst, with a long documented family connection and notable estate timber history.
connection: The family workbook says Elinor Loyd lived at Whiligh after marrying George Courthope, who was of Whiligh and Sprivers.
status: Whiligh and Courthopes remains a Grade II* listed house. Current ownership and estate operations are unverified; public access is not established.

paragraphs.heading: House and historical estate
paragraphs.text: Historic England dates the original portion of Whiligh and Courthopes to 1586 and notes early nineteenth-century additions and alterations around 1840. It also identifies it as a Courthope family home since 1512 and records historic timber links with Westminster Hall.

paragraphs.heading: Loyd family connection
paragraphs.text: The workbook connects Elinor Sarah Loyd to Whiligh through her 1876 marriage to George Courthope, and says she lived there and had eight children. The house therefore appears in this family history through marriage and residence; sources reviewed do not establish ownership by the Loyd family.

paragraphs.heading: Estate records and timber history
paragraphs.text: Wadhurst History Society's catalogue lists Courthope family/estate photographs, including haymaking at Whiligh around 1908. Catalogue descriptions establish the archival lead, not the contents of uninspected images. The workbook's Loyd connection is through Elinor's marriage and residence, not ownership.

paragraphs.heading: Whiligh archive and inheritance records
paragraphs.text: A Friends of the National Libraries account says George Campion Courthope inherited Whiligh with Sprivers in 1835, while his son George John married Elinor (“Lina”) Loyd in 1876; it says their children were raised at Sprivers. This establishes a family base at Sprivers but does not exclude residence at Whiligh in another period; the workbook’s specific Whiligh residence claim remains unverified. A 2025 Arts Council report describes the Courthope archive at East Sussex Record Office as an unusually complete estate archive from 1266–2012 with manorial records, early estate maps and personal papers; these catalogued holdings offer a direct research path, but no individual deed or tenancy record was inspected here.

paragraphs.heading: Whiligh archive and inheritance records
paragraphs.text: A 2007 survey of Sprivers Cottages reports that the Courthope Papers at East Sussex Record Office were consulted and cites deeds for the purchases that reunited separate Upper and Lower Sprivers holdings in 1700–1704. It also says the Sprivers estate passed to the National Trust under Robert Courthope’s will in 1966. These findings concern Sprivers and its cottages; they clarify the wider Courthope archive trail but do not establish Elinor’s residence at Whiligh.

name: Withybrook manor and estate
location: Withybrook and neighbouring Wolvey, Warwickshire, England
summary: The workbook places Lewis Vivian Loyd at Withybrook; a 1912 directory independently identifies Richard Loyd as lord of the manor and principal landowner.
connection: The workbook places Lewis Vivian Loyd at Withybrook; a 1912 directory independently identifies Richard Loyd as lord of the manor and principal landowner.
status: Current estate configuration unverified

paragraphs.heading: The Loyd holding in a contemporary directory
paragraphs.text: Kelly’s 1912 directory names Richard Loyd as lord of the manor and principal landowner. It separately lists Herbert Ingram at Overstone Lodge and farmer Thomas Dexter at Withybrook Hall. Together with the workbook’s residence reference, this establishes a substantial Loyd association with the area, but neither the Hall nor the Lodge should automatically be labelled Lewis Vivian Loyd’s home. The directory’s acreage describes the parish, not the estate.

paragraphs.heading: Medieval Withybrook
paragraphs.text: The scheduled medieval settlement includes the remains of a moat, buildings, fishponds and a mill landscape. Historic England records a twelfth-century chapel and land associated with Coombe Abbey, and medieval references to a millpond. An estate map of 1748 and tithe map of 1844 help document the later landscape. This history concerns the settlement and earthworks around the church; it does not establish a continuous descent of the later Loyd estate from every medieval holding.

paragraphs.heading: The 1918 sale record
paragraphs.text: Historic England catalogues particulars dated 21 June 1918 for the Wolvey and Withybrook estate, reference SC01190. Named holdings include Overstone Lodge, Withybrook House Farm, Hall Farm, Grange Farm, Dole Farm and Cloudesley Farm and Lodge, among others. The catalogue establishes the scope of the advertised sale, but the particulars themselves have not been inspected and no purchaser or completed disposal is established here.
